prompt: In the portal, somebody drags a new step into a workflow in the designer and saves. What did they change?
hint: The section calls the designer a view of something.

choices.text: A drawing that the service turns into a definition each time a run starts
choices.why: Nothing is regenerated per run. The definition is the thing saved, and the drawing is made from it.

choices.text: The workflow definition, a JSON document
choices.why: Yes. The designer edits the document, and the code view shows the same document as text.

choices.text: A Bicep file kept by the portal beside the workflow
choices.why: Bicep is how this lesson writes the resource. The portal keeps no Bicep; it compiles to the same JSON.

choices.text: A program in C# that the designer generates and compiles
choices.why: There is no generated program. Azure runs the definition as it is.

prompt: `Get_orders` fails on every retry one morning. `Any_orders` has `"runAfter": {"Get_orders": ["Succeeded"]}`. What happens to `Any_orders`?
hint: An action whose predecessor ended in a status it did not list does not run.

choices.text: It runs, with an empty body from `Get_orders`, and takes the else branch
choices.why: It would need `Failed` in its `runAfter` to run at all; it never evaluates its expression.

choices.text: It waits until the next morning's run, when `Get_orders` succeeds
choices.why: Each run is separate. Nothing carries over from one morning to the next.

choices.text: It is marked `Skipped`, and the run ends `Failed`
choices.why: Yes. The engine marks the failed action's successors `Skipped`, and a branch that ends in failure fails the run.

choices.text: It is retried with the same policy as `Get_orders`
choices.why: A retry policy belongs to the action that has one; `Any_orders` was never attempted.

prompt: An alert action should run only when `Get_orders` has failed. It names `Get_orders` with the status `Failed` in its `___` property.
hint: The same property gives every action in the lesson its place in the run.

prompt: In the lesson's run, which of these reached a compiled template exactly as written? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look for which builds printed nothing and which printed an error.

choices.text: A `runAfter` naming `Get_order`, an action that does not exist
choices.why: Yes: `typo.bicep` compiled with no warning. The definition's contents are not checked.

choices.text: The function name `lenght`, in both expressions that used it
choices.why: Yes: `grep -c` found it on two lines of `lenght.json`.

choices.text: The string `"no orders to send"` written in double quotes
choices.why: That one was refused: three errors, exit status 1, and no `quotes.json` at all.

choices.text: The `\'` inside each expression
choices.why: The backslashes are Bicep's escaping and are gone in the template, where a quote is a plain `'`.

prompt: A developer adds a top-level action `Archive` to the definition with `"runAfter": {}`, and leaves `Get_orders` as it is. When does `Archive` run?
hint: Two actions now have the same, empty, `runAfter`.

choices.text: After `Any_orders`, because it was added below it in the file
choices.why: Position in the file decides nothing: the actions are keys of an object.

choices.text: Before `Get_orders`, which then waits for it
choices.why: `Get_orders` waits for nothing but the trigger; its own `runAfter` did not change.

choices.text: As soon as the trigger fires, alongside `Get_orders`
choices.why: Yes. An empty `runAfter` means after the trigger, and two actions with nothing to wait for both start then.

choices.text: Never, because only one action in a definition may have an empty `runAfter`
choices.why: Nothing in the language says so; the true branch of `Any_orders` has its own action with an empty one.

prompt: The morning export sends its mail through the Office 365 Outlook connector, a managed one. Where is the connection to finance's mailbox, in a Consumption workflow?
hint: `outlook.json` holds it.

choices.text: Inside the definition, in the action's `inputs`
choices.why: The action only names it, through `@parameters('$connections')`; the connection is elsewhere.

choices.text: In a resource of its own, of type `Microsoft.Web/connections`
choices.why: Yes. An API connection is a separate Azure resource, in the same resource group and region as the workflow.

choices.text: In the Bicep parameter file, as a password
choices.why: Office 365 signs in with Entra ID. The service keeps tokens, not a password, and nothing of it is in a file.

choices.text: In a `connections.json` file beside the workflow
choices.why: That file belongs to built-in connections in a Standard logic app, not to a managed connector in Consumption.

prompt: `outlook.json` contains `[subscriptionResourceId(...)]` and `daily-orders.json` contains `@body('Get_orders')`. When is each one evaluated?
hint: One belongs to Resource Manager, the other to the workflow.

choices.text: Both by the Bicep compiler, when it writes the template
choices.why: The compiler wrote both into the template as text; it evaluated neither.

choices.text: Both by Resource Manager, at deployment
choices.why: Resource Manager evaluates the brackets and passes the `@` strings through untouched.

choices.text: The `@` one once at deployment, the bracketed one on every run
choices.why: That is the right pair of moments, given to the wrong expressions.

choices.text: The bracketed one once at deployment, the `@` one on every run
choices.why: Yes. ARM expressions are resolved by Resource Manager; workflow expressions by Logic Apps, each time a run reaches them.

prompt: A Consumption workflow starts from a polling trigger that checks a mailbox every 5 minutes, all day, and finds a new message twice. How many trigger checks are billed that day?
hint: A check that finds nothing is billed like one that finds something.

prompt: Match each need of the shop with the part of a workflow that meets it.
hint: One item on the right meets none of them.

pairs.left: start at six every morning, São Paulo time
start the moment the warehouse system posts a shipment
notice new files on a supplier's FTP server
survive the API answering 429 for a minute
pairs.right: a retry policy on the HTTP action

prompt: Months after it was set up, the morning email stops. In the run history `Get_orders` succeeded and `Send_export` failed with an authorisation error. The person who set up the workflow left the company last week. What is the likely cause?
hint: Somebody signed in once, when the connection was made.

choices.text: The connection needs authorising again
choices.why: Yes. It keeps tokens for whoever signed in, and they went with that person's account; the email stops until somebody authorises the connection again.

choices.text: The Outlook connector throttled the workflow
choices.why: Throttling answers 429 and is retried by the policy; it is not an authorisation error.

choices.text: The Recurrence trigger lost its time zone
choices.why: The run started and `Get_orders` succeeded, so the trigger did its part.

choices.text: The definition still refers to the old `$connections` value
choices.why: The definition names the connection by its resource id, which did not change when the person left.

prompt: What does `standard.bicep` declare to get a Standard logic app?
hint: `jq` printed two resources and their kind.

choices.text: A `Microsoft.Logic/workflows` resource with a larger `sku`
choices.why: That is Consumption's type, and it has no tier to raise: Standard is a different resource.

choices.text: A function app with a Logic Apps setting in `host.json`
choices.why: A Standard logic app is on the Functions runtime, but the file declares a plan and a site, with no `host.json`.

choices.text: A `WS1` plan and a `Microsoft.Web/sites` of kind `functionapp,workflowapp`
choices.why: Yes. It is declared the way a web app is: a plan of the Workflow Standard tier and a site on it.

choices.text: A container image of the Logic Apps runtime, and a Container App
choices.why: Nothing in the file is a container; the runtime comes with the site.

prompt: In a Consumption workflow, a `foreach` loop goes over 50 orders with two actions inside. How many executions does that loop bill?
hint: The documentation's example: 10 items with one action is 11.

prompt: Tuesday's email was empty. Put the steps of finding out why in order.
hint: Start from the list of runs and finish with the evidence.
items: see that `No_orders` ran and the true branch was `Skipped`
open `Get_orders` and read the output it received
find that the API answered with an empty array
trap: Which branch ran comes before why: the history shows `Skipped` on the branch first, and the HTTP output explains it.

prompt: Could the morning export be a stateless workflow in a Standard logic app, to make it cheaper?
hint: Look at how it starts.

choices.text: Yes, because the run lasts well under the five minutes a stateless run is given
choices.why: The duration fits, but the trigger does not.

choices.text: No: it would need a push trigger, and Recurrence is not one
choices.why: Yes. The documentation says the Recurrence trigger is available only for stateful workflows.

choices.text: No, because stateless workflows cannot call HTTP endpoints
choices.why: They can; what they do not do is poll a `202 Accepted` for the result.

choices.text: Yes, and its run history would be kept for 90 days as well
choices.why: A stateless workflow keeps its run details in memory, so there is no history unless it is turned on.

prompt: Monday's run failed in `Export`. On Tuesday you fix the definition, deploy it and resubmit Monday's run from the portal. What does the resubmitted run execute?
hint: The documentation lists what a resubmission keeps from the original.

choices.text: The fixed definition, with Monday's inputs
choices.why: That is what most people expect, and the documentation says otherwise.

choices.text: The fixed definition, with a fresh call to the shop's API
choices.why: A resubmission reuses the original run's inputs, and its definition too.

choices.text: Nothing: a failed run cannot be resubmitted
choices.why: A finished run, `Failed` included, can be resubmitted in a stateful workflow.

choices.text: Monday's version of the definition, with Monday's inputs
choices.why: Yes. The rerun uses the workflow version of the original run, even after an update, so the fix is tested by a new run.

prompt: In this course, what can a laptop check about the Consumption workflow in `daily-orders.bicep`?
hint: Think of what the misspelt copies showed.

choices.text: That every `runAfter` names an action that exists
choices.why: `typo.bicep` named one that does not, and compiled clean.

choices.text: The resource, and nothing inside the definition
choices.why: Yes. The compiler checks the resource's properties; the definition is a value of any shape to it.

choices.text: That the expressions call functions that exist
choices.why: `lenght` reached the template twice.

choices.text: A whole run, against a local copy of the Logic Apps runtime
choices.why: Only Standard has a local runtime, through Visual Studio Code, and this course does not use it.

prompt: A Consumption workflow writes one line for each order: a `foreach` over the orders with three actions inside. On a day of 1,500 orders, how many executions does the loop bill in that run?
hint: Items times actions, plus the loop.

prompt: To try a run without calling the shop's API, an action can be marked to return a mock output instead. The definition keeps those mock outputs under the top-level key `___`.
hint: It sits beside `triggers`, `actions` and `parameters`, and its name says the outputs do not change.

prompt: A workflow and a function are used together. Which division of the work does the lesson describe as common?
hint: Each side keeps what it is good at.

choices.text: The function runs the schedule and calls the workflow for every record
choices.why: That puts the loop on the side that bills per step, which is the arrangement to avoid.

choices.text: The workflow does the logic and the function only sends the email
choices.why: Sending mail is what a connector already does; that is the half the workflow is for.

choices.text: A function does the looping step; the workflow keeps the rest
choices.why: Yes. The workflow keeps the schedule, the connectors and the history; its Function action calls the function, and a step that would cost thousands of executions is one call.

choices.text: Each runs the whole job, and the cheaper one is kept after a month
choices.why: Running a job twice for a month is a comparison, not a division of work.

prompt: Each night the shop wants loyalty points worked out for 40,000 customers, with rules the developers change every month and want tested before release. Which fits?
hint: Count the steps, and ask whose logic it is.

choices.text: A Consumption workflow with a `foreach` over the customers
choices.why: Tens of thousands of iterations billed per action, and rules that cannot be tested on a laptop.

choices.text: A stateless Standard workflow, to avoid storing history
choices.why: A stateless workflow cannot start on a schedule, and 40,000 records exceed its `foreach` default of 100 items.

choices.text: Code: a timer-triggered function, or Durable Functions
choices.why: Yes. The steps are the shop's own logic, the volume is large, and the rules need tests: all three point at code.

choices.text: A Consumption workflow that sends each customer to the HTTP action of a second workflow
choices.why: That doubles the workflows and still bills every customer as several executions.

prompt: Match each job with what the lesson would run it on.
hint: One item on the right fits none of the jobs.

pairs.left: a CSV of the orders mailed to finance each morning
a workflow that must reach a database inside a VNet
an order process with the shop's own rules, tested in CI
the shop's order API, answering requests

right_distractors: a stateless workflow with a Recurrence trigger

prompt: A definition gives `Summary` the `runAfter` `{"Export": ["Failed"]}`. On a morning when `Export` succeeds, what happens to `Summary`?
hint: `runAfter` lists the statuses that let an action run.

choices.text: It runs, because `Export` finished
choices.why: Finishing is not enough: the status has to be one of those listed.

choices.text: It does not run: `Succeeded` is not in its list
choices.why: Yes. Only `Failed` lets it run, which is the shape of an alert rather than of a summary.

choices.text: It runs before `Export`, to be ready if it fails
choices.why: `runAfter` only ever makes an action wait; it never moves one earlier.

choices.text: `bicep build` refuses the file, since `Failed` is not a status
choices.why: `Failed` is one of the four statuses, and the compiler does not read the definition anyway.

prompt: At 06:00 the shop's API is down for 90 seconds. `Get_orders` has the lesson's retry policy: fixed, 3 retries, one minute apart. Put what happens in order.
hint: The API is back between the first retry and the second.
items: the first call of `Get_orders` gets a 503
a minute later, the first retry gets a 503
a minute after that, the second retry gets the orders
trap: The third retry never happens: the second one succeeded, so `Get_orders` is billed as three executions, not four.

prompt: `bicep build daily-orders.bicep` printed nothing and wrote `daily-orders.json`. What does that establish?
hint: Separate the resource from the workflow inside it.

choices.text: That the workflow will run correctly once deployed
choices.why: Nothing in the definition was checked, so the compile says nothing about a run.

choices.text: That Azure has accepted the template
choices.why: Nothing was sent to Azure; the compile happened on the laptop, with no subscription.

choices.text: That the resource fits the published type for its API version
choices.why: Yes, and only that: `definition` is any value to the compiler, as the misspelt copies showed.

choices.text: That every expression parses, though not that its functions exist
choices.why: The expressions are strings to the compiler; it parsed none of them.
